stem: Which approach gives the most reliable picture of whether a website works for screen reader users?

options.text: Observe screen reader users on real tasks and note if they get stuck.
options.rationale: Watching people use the site on real tasks reveals problems that automated checks and source inspection miss.

options.text: Count how many images on the site have an alt attribute.
options.rationale: Counting attributes measures markup coverage, not whether the text alternatives are useful or the site is usable.

options.text: Run a screen reader over the home page and time how long it takes to read it.
options.rationale: Reading speed does not show whether users can find information, follow the reading order, or complete tasks.

options.text: Set the screen reader to its fastest speech rate and listen for errors.
options.rationale: Listening at speed tests the reviewer's comprehension, not the experience of people who use screen readers daily.

explanation: Watching people who use screen readers complete realistic tasks reveals problems that automated checks miss, including confusing reading order, unclear names, and unexpected focus changes. Counting alt attributes or timing a page read does not show whether the site is usable.

references.title: W3C WAI — Involving Users in Evaluating Web Accessibility

author: Oxypteros
